## Source map — GOV-003

**Document:** *Fourth-quarter 2022 public finances and debt*  
**Issuer:** Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público (SHCP), Mexico  
**Publication date:** 30 January 2023  
**Period covered:** Primarily full-year 2022, with quarter-, month-, and year-to-date comparisons.  
**Source role:** Executive official report. The extract presents SHCP’s institutional account; figures are not independently verified here.  
**Chapter relevance:** 5B.1, 5B.3, 5B.6, 5B.7, 5B.8, 5B.9, 5B.10.

### Atomic claims

| ID | Evidence type | Claim and qualification | Locator |
|---|---|---|---|
| GOV-003-01 | Official assertion | SHCP states that public finances were responsibly managed, debt remained stable, and spending was efficiently exercised toward family welfare at the end of the administration’s fourth year. | Block 1, opening paragraph |
| GOV-003-02 | Reported figure / official framing | Public debt was **49.4% of GDP** in 2022, reported as **1.6 percentage points below the budgeted level** and **1.4 points below 2021**. The extract does not specify whether this is gross/net debt or the precise public-sector perimeter. | Block 1, paragraph 2 |
| GOV-003-03 | Reported figure | Economic growth accumulated to **2.9% through November 2022**, described as better than analysts expected. This is not presented as a final full-year growth rate. | Block 2, paragraph 1 |
| GOV-003-04 | Reported labor outcome | At year-end, unemployment was reported at **2.8% overall** and **2.5% for women**; employment increased by **2.4 million jobs in 2022**, “mostly formal.” The extract does not define the employment series or establish ruler attribution. | Block 2, paragraph 2 |
| GOV-003-05 | Reported macro/social indicator | Private consumption grew **7.1% through October 2022**, more than twice its stated historical average; services consumption had recovered pre-pandemic levels. | Block 2, paragraph 3; Block 3, paragraph 1 |
| GOV-003-06 | Reported investment outcome | Gross fixed investment grew **5.5% year-on-year through October**, versus a **1.6% historical average** for the same period; machinery and equipment grew **12.2%**, versus a **5.0% historical average**. | Block 3, paragraph 1 |
| GOV-003-07 | Reported labor outcome | Average annual unemployment was **3.3%** in 2022. The IMSS registered **753,000 new jobs**, mainly permanent; real average wages rose **2.7% annually**. | Block 3, paragraphs 2–3 |
| GOV-003-08 | Official comparison | From December 2018 to December 2022, **1.3 million IMSS jobs** were created, mostly permanent; SHCP says this exceeded the equivalent totals under the Felipe Calderón and Vicente Fox administrations. The comparison basis and underlying series are not supplied in the extract. | Block 3, paragraph 4 |
| GOV-003-09 | Reported external-sector figure | 2022 foreign trade reached a reported historical maximum of **US$1.2 trillion**, driven especially by manufactured exports and intermediate/capital-goods imports. New FDI reached **US$14 billion**, described as the second-highest amount after 2013. | Block 3, paragraph 5 |
| GOV-003-10 | Official attribution | SHCP attributes stronger revenues partly to oil prices, tax-evasion enforcement, and higher real wages, while stating that no new taxes were created. These are institutional explanations, not independently established causal findings. | Block 4, paragraphs 2–6 |
| GOV-003-11 | Reported fiscal figure | Public revenues totaled **MXN 6.595 trillion**, **MXN 422 billion above program**, and increased **2.5%** from 2021. Federal-government revenues were **MXN 632 billion above program**, including **MXN 397 billion associated with lower revenue from the fuel IEPS stimulus**. | Block 4, paragraphs 1–2 |
| GOV-003-12 | Reported fiscal composition | Oil revenues were **MXN 1.482 trillion**, equal to **5.2% of GDP**, up **18.7% in real annual terms** from 2021. Tax revenue excluding fuel IEPS reached **13.6% of GDP**, up **7.8% real year-on-year**. ISR was **MXN 2.270 trillion / 8.0% of GDP**, with **11% annual growth**; VAT was **MXN 1.222 trillion / 4.3% of GDP**. | Block 4, paragraphs 3–7 |
| GOV-003-13 | Reported expenditure figure | Public spending increased **4.1% in real annual terms** to **MXN 7.569 trillion / 26.5% of GDP**. Social-protection spending increased **8.7% real** to **5.3% of GDP**. Physical investment increased **25.2%**, reaching **3.3% of GDP**. | Block 5, paragraphs 1–3 |
| GOV-003-14 | Reported fiscal balance | The primary balance was a **deficit of 0.5% of GDP**; the public deficit was **3.4%**; Public-Sector Borrowing Requirements were **4.4%**. | Block 5, paragraph 5 |
| GOV-003-15 | Official resilience claim | SHCP reports fiscal buffers totaling **US$262 billion**, including international reserves, the IMF Flexible Credit Line, the Federal Reserve swap line, and stabilization funds. The extract gives no eligibility, availability, or accounting details. | Block 5, paragraph 6 |
| GOV-003-16 | Debt-operation record | On 7 October, SHCP reported a **MXN 68.017 billion debt buyback** for maturities from 2023–2046 alongside **MXN 48.596 billion** in long-term Bond and Udibonos sales; later operations included Bondes G and Bono M placements and additional Bono M transactions. | Block 6, paragraphs 1–4 |
| GOV-003-17 | Official forward-looking claim | SHCP states that debt pressures for 2023 and the following two years were reduced by an average **73%** through buybacks, releasing **US$3 billion** for the next administration. The calculation method and baseline are absent. | Block 6, paragraph 5 |
| GOV-003-18 | Official reputation claim | SHCP reports 21 international recognitions over four years and says Mexico retained investment grade with stable outlooks from all eight rating agencies evaluating the debt. No agencies or recognitions are identified in the extract. | Block 6, paragraph 6 |

### Limitations and unresolved issues

- The extract does not state whether accounts are cash-, accrual-, or mixed-basis; nominal versus real treatment is specified only for selected growth rates.
- Debt coverage, gross/net status, currency composition, debt service, maturity-risk profile, guarantees, arrears, SOEs, and quasi-fiscal liabilities are not provided.
- No auditor opinion, audit status, revision/restatement note, methodology appendix, assumptions table, or explicit fiscal-rule compliance statement appears.
- “Program” is not defined as original or revised. Spending execution and budgeted-versus-actual composition are not shown.
- Reported improvements may reflect oil prices, inflation, timing, or one-off debt transactions; the extract does not resolve these possibilities.
- No contrary external material is included. Internally adverse material consists of the primary and public deficits, PSBR, dependence on high oil prices, and the fuel-tax subsidy effect on revenue presentation. | Blocks 4–5
- The page directs readers to detailed finance/debt statistics, but those materials are not part of this extract. | Block 6, final paragraph; Block 7

### Stronger-model reopen list

Reopen the detailed statistical annexes for debt perimeter and basis, original versus revised program, execution and capital-spending composition, debt-service/maturity/currency data, audit or provisional status, the 73% debt-pressure calculation, the US$262 billion buffer composition, and the eight rating-agency/21-recognition claims. No legal authority, amendment, procedural status, exception, or effective date is cited in the extract.
